analysis.one_liner: Expands voter registration and early voting, makes Election Day a holiday, and requires disclosure of big-money political spending.
analysis.headline: All 50 cosponsors were Senate Democrats and independents, but the bill never got a vote: it sat in the Rules Committee from July 2023 until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require states to automatically and same-day register voters, offer early voting and no-excuse mail voting, make Election Day a federal holiday, and restore federal voting rights to people who are out of prison. It would also require paper ballots with post-election audits, protect election workers, generally ban mid-decade congressional redistricting, require disclosure of political spending including online ads, close loopholes that let foreign money into elections, and create an optional small-dollar public funding program for House races.
analysis.who_benefits: All eligible voters, especially hourly workers who can't take time off on a Tuesday, voters with disabilities, voters on purged rolls, and citizens who finished felony sentences. Small-dollar donors would gain matching public funds, and voters in gerrymandered districts would gain from the mid-decade redistricting ban.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, especially hourly workers and small donors

how_it_helps.text: Requires automatic registration through motor vehicle agencies, online registration, and same-day registration in federal elections [S2][S3].
Requires early voting, no-excuse voting by mail, secured drop boxes, and makes Election Day a legal public holiday [S2][S3].
Restores federal voting rights to citizens not currently serving a felony sentence, affecting the roughly 4.6 million Americans disenfranchised by past convictions cited in the bill's findings [S3].
Requires voter-verifiable paper ballots, post-election audits, protections for election workers against harassment, and new crimes for interfering with registration or certification [S2][S3].
Generally prohibits mid-decade congressional redistricting and sets criteria to curb partisan gerrymandering [S2][S3].
Requires disclosure of campaign spending including online political ads, closes loopholes in the ban on foreign-national spending, and restricts super PAC-candidate coordination [S2][S3].
Creates an optional program of public 'democracy credits' and small-dollar matching for House candidates, plus childcare as an allowed campaign expense for candidates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large donors and groups that spend untraceable money on elections would lose the anonymity and coordination room the bill eliminates. Digital platforms would face new political-ad transparency requirements. Taxpayers would fund roughly $3 billion in registration grants plus the small-dollar campaign financing program. State election offices would bear implementation costs and the loss of control over election rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, platforms, taxpayers, state election offices

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts many state election rules, replacing state-by-state voting procedures with uniform federal mandates for federal elections, which critics call a federal takeover of election administration that states have historically controlled [S2][S3].
It authorizes $3 billion in registration grants and creates a publicly funded campaign financing system for House races, which critics oppose as taxpayer-funded political campaigns [S3].

Automatic registration shifts a large implementation burden onto state motor-vehicle and election agencies, and the bill itself acknowledges error risk by shielding people from prosecution or immigration consequences when agencies register them by mistake [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The voting-access and election-security provisions address real barriers that fall hardest on hourly workers, disabled voters, and communities of color, and the transparency provisions target a documented loophole in foreign-money and dark-money rules. The main honest costs are the money (billions in grants plus public campaign financing), a genuine federalism tradeoff in standardizing elections nationwide, and implementation risk in automatic registration. On balance the bill is designed to widen participation and shrink the role of concentrated money; its flaws are cost and design details rather than a transfer of benefits away from ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Rules and Administration Committee in July 2023, the committee never voted on it, and the Senate never brought it to the floor, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Klobuchar introduced the Freedom to Vote Act on July 18, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration [S5].
Fifty senators cosponsored the bill: 47 of 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 4 Senate independents; no Republican cosponsored [S4].

The action history shows no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill still stuck in committee [S5][S1].

A nearly identical predecessor bill failed in January 2022 when a procedural vote to cut off debate got only 49 of the 60 votes needed, after two senators refused to set the 60-vote rule aside; with the same 60-vote threshold in place in 2023-2024 and no Republican support, the bill had no realistic path even if it had reached the floor (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The groups the bill would have constrained are better off because it never moved: large campaign donors and untraceable-spending groups keep the current rules, party mapmakers can redraw districts mid-decade, and states keep sole control over voting procedures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors, dark-money groups, party mapmakers

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.role: Senator from Minnesota; sponsor and chair of the Rules and Administration Committee it was referred to
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the full Democratic caucus plus independents as cosponsors; her committee took no further action on it

for.name: 3 of 4 Senate Independents
for.role: Independent senators, including Manchin and Sinema

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor during the 118th Congress; the record shows no floor action after referral [S5]

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and the conference uniformly opposed its predecessor, which failed a 60-vote procedural vote 49-51 in January 2022

against.name: Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin
against.role: Senate independents (Sinema I-AZ, Manchin D-WV; Manchin a cosponsor of this bill)
against.what_they_did: In January 2022 refused to end the Senate's 60-vote filibuster rule to pass the predecessor voting bill, which is why the same measure had no path to passage in the 118th Congress even with their cosponsorship here

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent, no Republican supported it, and the predecessor bill failed 49-51 on a party-line procedural vote in 2022.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and dark-money spending groups
industries.note: The bill would require disclosure of political spending including online ads, close foreign-money loopholes, and restrict super PAC-candidate coordination, shrinking the influence of untraceable money in elections. Their interest in avoiding disclosure runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays for campaign messages [S2][S3].

The bill generally bans mid-decade congressional redistricting and sets neutral criteria for districting, limiting the ability of the party holding a state government to redraw maps for its own advantage. Incumbents' interest in protected districts runs against voters' interest in competitive representation [S2][S3].

Online platforms would have to display and preserve sponsor disclaimers on political ads, and campaigns would face new spending reports. The industry's interest in lighter ad rules runs against the public's interest in knowing who is behind political messages [S3].

Paper-ballot and audit mandates would force replacement of some voting systems, but the bill authorizes grants for compliant systems and security upgrades, so the same companies would be paid to make the changes [S3].

The bill lets party committees raise small-dollar funds in separate accounts and gives participating House candidates public matching support, strengthening parties' ties to small donors rather than large ones [S3].
